trecho.0: tejo Navas, Roland Campos, Angélica Madeira, Bené Fonteles and Marília Panitz produced an important body of reflections that accompany this compilation of records that survived time. It is possible, in this way, to travel here through twenty years of history by means of the projects and installations: “Experiência Tumulto (1985)”, “Cubo Cruz Lápide (1985)”, “O Profeta e a Jaguatirica (1985-86)”, “DO AKD-MICO AO POLE-MICO (1986)”, “Mognus Dei (1990)”, “O Sol de Goethe (1999)”, “São João Beuys (1990)”, “Ser ou não Ser, Ao Gullar (1993)”, “Pega Manet/De Onde Vem A Escuridão (1986)”, “TV Anal (1999)”, “Hermógenes (1999)”, “Obranome (2003)” and “Cultura X Natureza = Barbárie (1998/2005)” Marília Panitz, in her text “To What Matters, an Answer”, proposes an itinerary for reading Barja’s works, starting from the concept of equation, so dear to the artist. In the “enigmas of visual equations” of Barja’s commentaries-constructions, the author highlights the condensation of meanings that has humour as its tool. Appropriating the sharp steel of irony, armed with a laughter of Oswaldian inspiration, the anthropophagous Barja, under a “strong influence of the neoconcrete movement” composes a set of installations in which
trecho.1: installation “São João Beuys”, draws attention to the infinity of associations and meanings existing between the immortal and charismatic political agitators that Saint John the Baptist and Joseph Beuys were. Angélica Madeira highlights the influence of surrealism and dada in this work, in which coexist the playful, of a supposedly unpretentious humour, and the gravity of the materials, above all the mutton fat which, under the action of light, solidifies and liquefies over the course of the day, causing strangeness and unease. Eygene Bavcar, blind since the age of eleven, sets himself “to the listening of a painting” and plunges into the universe of “Hermógenes” and of “O Sol de Goethe”. Bavcar is interested above all in the white cane, one of the objects that make up “Hermógenes”; it becomes “the invisible canvas, the painting to be created (...) the brush over the darkness”. What Barja paints, in composing the space, is the “difficult path of the invisible”, penetrable, perhaps, by the forms that the artist formulates. Mercedes Replinger, together with Marília Panitz, is the one who examines the whole of Wagner Barja’s oeuvre. trecho.2: An operation of dismantling the work in its own construction (it is there, precarious, on the verge of coming undone for holding what cannot occupy the same place — water and electricity, since the submerged image shows itself on television screens). These aquarium-boxes, which carry other boxes (aquarium?), produce their own equation that the artist formulates as nature X culture = barbarism, his own formulation of circularity: who looks at whom? Who is the referent? Where does the proposal begin? And is this not the equation without an answer produced by art, at the very least since Velasquez? The opaque eyes of “Hermógenes”: The story of being introduced to the world by a blind grandfather may imply the habit of “guessing vision” or of exercising it with closed eyes, reinventing the world. The story of recalling the world (through reading) to a blind grandfather may imply a re-elaboration of things through the word, a certain subjection of reality to another (also) imaginary order. All these figures present this same coincidence: light and vision arise from a blind centre. All of them manifest, as in the flame, that any luminous effect at a dark centre is opaque in its interior. As if its negation, or its inevitable relation with its opposite, were consubstantial to light. As Derrida would say, the hypothesis of sight passes, in reality, through the cancellation of the gaze, its épochè, that is, its interruption or suspension (13). “Hermógenes” (1999) speaks to us of this interruption of vision. I think that, since the Greeks, it has been forgotten or hidden by the progress of a vision that claims to see everything, without knowing anything or without representing to itself what it has seen” (15). The blind man can cross through images, the reality that surrounds us, and find, in this journey through darkness, other figures, other expressions that would be closer to the mythical and originating substrate of the world. In the dark cavity of their own body, the blind and the spectators who, temporarily blind, move through the installation “Hermógenes” (1999) can catch the light and draw in its interior figures, other forms that appear in close relation to the nocturnal imaginary. The spectator reproduces, then, an autonomous process of gestation of images that is not necessarily mediated by the gaze. In fact, the blindness imposed in “Hermógenes” (1999) presents itself as a model of thought, in a sense very similar to what Descartes proposes when he notes that the dark chamber was the demonstration of how an observer can know the world solely through the perception of the mind. trecho.8: Hermógenes (1999 possessing an eye specifically designed for contemplating the sun. Called the pineal eye, this gland is situated beneath the cranial crown and, unlike ordinary eyes fixed on the horizontality of day-today events available to their sight, permits us to rise up and see the sun face to face, like the eagle of the ancients. For Bataille, the pineal eye confirms the human being’s fervor to transcend his earthly condition.
